claim: During perceptual decision-making tasks, centroparietal electroencephalographic (EEG) potentials report an evidence accumulation-to-bound process that is time locked to trial onset.
source: During perceptual decision-making tasks, centroparietal electroencephalographic (EEG) potentials report an evidence accumulation-to-bound process that is time locked to trial onset.
evidence: This is a statement about established findings in the field, supported by the broader literature context.

claim: Decisions in real-world environments are rarely confined to discrete trials; they instead unfold continuously, with accumulation of time-varying evidence being recency-weighted towards its immediate past.
source: However, decisions in real-world environments are rarely confined to discrete trials; they instead unfold continuously, with accumulation of time-varying evidence being recency-weighted towards its immediate past.
evidence: This is a general statement about naturalistic decision-making that draws from established understanding in the field.

claim: The centroparietal positivity (CPP) becomes more sensitive to fluctuations in sensory evidence when large shifts in evidence are less frequent.
source: We show that adaptations in evidence weighting to these different environments are reflected in changes in the CPP. The CPP becomes more sensitive to fluctuations in sensory evidence when large shifts in evidence are less frequent
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study comparing RARE vs FREQUENT conditions.

claim: The CPP is primarily sensitive to fluctuations in decision-relevant (not decision-irrelevant) sensory input.
source: the potential is primarily sensitive to fluctuations in decision-relevant (not decision-irrelevant) sensory input.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the control experiment with vertical motion (Figure 8).

claim: A complementary triphasic component over occipito-parietal cortex encodes the sum of recently accumulated sensory evidence.
source: A complementary triphasic component over occipito-parietal cortex encodes the sum of recently accumulated sensory evidence
evidence: This is supported by the deconvolutional GLM analysis showing TRFs to continuous evidence.

claim: The magnitude of the triphasic component covaries with parameters describing how different individuals integrate sensory evidence over time.
source: its magnitude covaries with parameters describing how different individuals integrate sensory evidence over time.
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral-neural correlation analysis shown in Figure 9.

claim: A shift in decision threshold between different environments is reflected in the magnitude of pre-decision EEG activity.
source: A computational model based on leaky evidence accumulation suggests that these findings can be accounted for by a shift in decision threshold between different environments, which is also reflected in the magnitude of pre-decision EEG activity.
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling and EEG data showing pre-response differences between conditions.

claim: Optimising leaky evidence accumulation involves adapting one's behaviour to the overall statistics of the environment by changing the rate at which previous evidence is leaked (the 'decay') and the amount of cumulative evidence required before a categorical decision is made (the 'decision threshold').
source: Optimising leaky evidence accumulation involves adapting one's behaviour to the overall statistics of the environment. This can be achieved by changing the rate at which previous evidence is leaked (the 'decay') and the amount of cumulative evidence required before a categorical decision is made (the 'decision threshold') (Glaze et al., 2015; Kilpatrick et al., 2019; Veliz-Cuba et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work in the field.

claim: Humans can adapt the decay and decision threshold of sensory evidence accumulation to different dynamic environments.
source: While it is known that humans (Ganupuru et al., 2019; Glaze et al., 2018; Harun et al., 2020; Ossmy et al., 2013) and other animals (Levi et al., 2018; Piet et al., 2018) can adapt the decay and decision threshold of sensory evidence accumulation to different dynamic environments
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Other animals can adapt the decay and decision threshold of sensory evidence accumulation to different dynamic environments.
source: While it is known that humans (Ganupuru et al., 2019; Glaze et al., 2018; Harun et al., 2020; Ossmy et al., 2013) and other animals (Levi et al., 2018; Piet et al., 2018) can adapt the decay and decision threshold of sensory evidence accumulation to different dynamic environments
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior animal research.

claim: The centroparietal positivity (CPP) shows accumulator-like dynamics during decision formation.
source: Two of the best-studied human electroencephalographic (EEG) correlates of decision formation are an effector-independent centroparietal positivity (CPP) that shows accumulator-like dynamics during decision formation (Kelly and O'Connell, 2013; O'Connell et al., 2012; Pisauro et al., 2017; Twomey et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior EEG research.

claim: Motor preparation signals emerge prior to a response during decision-making.
source: and motor preparation signals that emerge prior to a response (Donner et al., 2009; Steinemann et al., 2018; Wyart et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on motor preparation.

claim: CPP amplitude at the time of making a response is increased by emphasising speed over accuracy.
source: For example, CPP amplitude at the time of making a response is increased by emphasising speed over accuracy (Steinemann et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Pre-trial motor lateralisation can reflect the prior expectation of a leftward or rightward action in the upcoming trial.
source: while pre-trial motor lateralisation can reflect the prior expectation of a leftward or rightward action in the upcoming trial (de Lange et al., 2013; Kelly et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Participants were less likely to detect response periods when these were RARE than when they were FREQUENT.
source: Examining the effects of response period frequency, participants were less likely (F(1,23) = 41.99, p=1.30 * 10–6) and slower (F(1,23) = 83.24, p=6.23 * 10–9) to detect response periods when these were RARE (blue lines in Figure 2b and c) than when they were FREQUENT (red lines in Figure 2b and c).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data and shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Participants were slower to detect response periods when these were RARE than when they were FREQUENT.
source: Examining the effects of response period frequency, participants were less likely (F(1,23) = 41.99, p=1.30 * 10–6) and slower (F(1,23) = 83.24, p=6.23 * 10–9) to detect response periods when these were RARE (blue lines in Figure 2b and c) than when they were FREQUENT (red lines in Figure 2b and c).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of reaction time data and shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Significantly more cumulative evidence was required for RARE than FREQUENT response periods, stretching back up to 3.5 s prior to the commitment to a response.
source: Indeed, when we examined the 'integration kernel' of average sensory evidence for successful responses, significantly more cumulative evidence was required for RARE than FREQUENT response periods, stretching back up to 3.5 s prior to the commitment to a response (Figure 2d; F-test with permutation-based correction for multiple comparisons, p<0.05).
evidence: This is supported by integration kernel analysis shown in Figure 2d with statistical testing.

claim: Participants detected response periods more frequently when these were LONG than when they were SHORT.
source: We also found that participants detected response periods more frequently when these were LONG than when they were SHORT (Figure 2b; F(1,23) = 178.52, p=2.51 * 10–12).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of detection rates shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Participants were slightly more conservative in their responding when trials were LONG, as shown by a longer average reaction time for LONG response periods relative to SHORT.
source: In fact, participants were slightly more conservative in their responding when trials were LONG, as shown by a longer average reaction time for LONG response periods relative to SHORT (even when restricting this analysis to focus on LONG responses that were less than 3.5 s, the maximum possible SHORT response duration including 500 ms response tolerance period; Figure 2c; F(1,23) = 70.00, p=2.78 * 10–8).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of reaction times shown in Figure 2c.

claim: There was a lower overall frequency of false alarms in LONG versus SHORT conditions.
source: We found that despite the structure of the noise stream being identical across the four conditions, there was a lower overall frequency of false alarms in LONG versus SHORT conditions (Figure 3a; F(1,23) = 58.67, p=8.98 * 10–8).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of false alarm rates shown in Figure 3a.

claim: There was no effect of response period frequency on false alarm rate.
source: There was no effect of response period frequency on false alarm rate (F(1,23) = 0.37, p=0.55).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of false alarm rates.

claim: The recovered evidence integration kernels from false alarms showed exponential decay weighting.
source: We tested this by calculating integration kernels derived from these responses. We found the recovered evidence integration kernels showed exponential decay weighting
evidence: This is supported by analysis of integration kernels from false alarm responses.

claim: Evidence accumulation was more temporally extended when response periods were RARE rather than FREQUENT.
source: We found the recovered evidence integration kernels showed exponential decay weighting, implying that participants were indeed performing continuous evidence integration throughout baseline periods as well as response periods, and that evidence accumulation was more temporally extended when response periods were RARE rather than FREQUENT (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by integration kernel analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The exponential decay model provided a good fit to data at a single-subject level (median R2 = 0.82, 95% confidence intervals for R2 = [0.42,0.93]).
source: Our exponential decay model provided a good fit to data at a single-subject level (median R2 = 0.82, 95% confidence intervals for R2 = [0.42,0.93]; see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for example fits)
evidence: This is supported by model fitting statistics and example fits shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The amplitude parameter A did not differ between RARE and FREQUENT conditions.
source: but A did not differ between these conditions (paired T(23) = 0.03, p=0.97; Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: When response periods were LONG rather than SHORT, the optimal adjustment was to reduce the amount of leak in the model, so that incoming sensory evidence persisted for longer within the decision variable.
source: This demonstrated that when response periods were LONG rather than SHORT, the optimal adjustment was to reduce the amount of leak in the model, so that incoming sensory evidence persisted for longer within the decision variable.
evidence: This is based on computational modeling results analyzing optimal parameters.

claim: When response periods were RARE rather than FREQUENT, the model could be optimised by increasing the decision threshold.
source: When response periods were RARE rather than FREQUENT, the model could be optimised by increasing the decision threshold.
evidence: This is based on computational modeling results analyzing optimal parameters.

claim: The amplitude of the integration kernel A was affected by manipulations of both θ and λ.
source: By contrast, we found that the amplitude of the integration kernel A was affected by manipulations of both θ and λ.
evidence: This is based on computational modeling analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The two regressors that reflected changes in the sensory evidence ('jump events') and the magnitude of |Δevidence| both elicited positive-going scalp topographies over centroparietal electrodes, peaking ~300 ms after this change occurred.
source: In particular, the two regressors that reflected changes in the sensory evidence ('jump events') and the magnitude of |Δevidence| both elicited positive-going scalp topographies over centroparietal electrodes, peaking ~300 ms after this change occurred (Figure 6a and b).
evidence: This is supported by the deconvolutional GLM analysis shown in Figure 6a and b.

claim: The scalp topography, timecourse, and reporting of |Δevidence| are consistent with the P300 component.
source: This scalp topography, timecourse, and reporting of |Δevidence| are consistent with the P300 component (Donchin, 1981; Duncan-Johnson and Donchin, 1977; Mars et al., 2008; Squires et al., 1976).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with cited literature on the P300 component.

claim: The scalp topography is consistent with the CPP.
source: The scalp topography is also consistent with the CPP (Kelly and O'Connell, 2013; O'Connell et al., 2012; O'Connell and Kelly, 2021)
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with cited literature on the CPP.

claim: The continuous |evidence| regressor elicited a triphasic potential over centroparietal electrodes.
source: In addition, the continuous |evidence| regressor elicited a triphasic potential over centroparietal electrodes (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is supported by the deconvolutional GLM analysis shown in Figure 6c.

claim: The triphasic potential is notably similar to EEG potentials reflecting 'decision update' signals during trial-based tasks that require integration of multiple, discrete pieces of evidence.
source: This triphasic potential is notably similar to EEG potentials reflecting 'decision update' signals during trial-based tasks that require integration of multiple, discrete pieces of evidence (Wyart et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with cited literature.

claim: The centroparietal response to the same change in sensory evidence was larger when response periods were RARE than when they were FREQUENT.
source: Indeed, we found that the centroparietal response to the same change in sensory evidence was larger when response periods were RARE than when they were FREQUENT (Figure 7a, Figure 7—figure supplement 2; p=0.017, cluster-based permutation test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of EEG data shown in Figure 7a.

claim: When making a correct response, preparatory motor activity over central electrodes reached a larger decision threshold for RARE versus FREQUENT response periods.
source: In addition, when making a correct response, preparatory motor activity over central electrodes reached a larger decision threshold for RARE versus FREQUENT response periods (Figure 7b; p=0.041, cluster-based permutation test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of EEG data shown in Figure 7b.

claim: Beta desynchronisation was greater in RARE than FREQUENT response periods.
source: We found similar effects in beta-band desynchronisation prior, averaged over the same electrodes; beta desynchronisation was greater in RARE than FREQUENT response periods.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of beta-band activity.

claim: There was no statistically significant difference for either of these regressors between SHORT versus LONG response periods.
source: By contrast, we found no statistically significant difference for either of these regressors between SHORT versus LONG response periods (Figure 7—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: Centroparietal responses reflected both 'jump events' and their associated |Δevidence| for decision-relevant motion, but these were substantially reduced for regressors that reflected changes in decision-irrelevant evidence.
source: As in the main experiment, we found that centroparietal responses reflected both 'jump events' and their associated |Δevidence| for decision-relevant motion, but these were substantially reduced for regressors that reflected changes in decision-irrelevant evidence (Figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by the control experiment data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The across-subject correlation between the triphasic potential and τ replicated across all four independent conditions.
source: Although this across-subject correlation was discovered via exploratory analyses, it replicated across all four independent conditions, substantially increasing the likelihood of it being a true positive result (response periods FREQUENT and SHORT: Spearman's ρ = –0.45, p=0.027; FREQUENT and LONG: ρ = –0.52, p=0.0099; RARE and SHORT: ρ = –0.53, p=0.0080; RARE and LONG: ρ = –0.46, p=0.025).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis across all four conditions.

claim: There was no evidence for an across-subject correlation between fitted integration decay time constants and EEG regressors encoding evidence updates at jump events (Δevidence).
source: By contrast, we found no evidence for an across-subject correlation between fitted integration decay time constants and EEG regressors encoding evidence updates at jump events (Δevidence), nor between fitted amplitude parameters (A) and any EEG regressors.
evidence: This is a negative result from correlation analysis.

claim: There was no evidence for an across-subject correlation between fitted amplitude parameters (A) and any EEG regressors.
source: By contrast, we found no evidence for an across-subject correlation between fitted integration decay time constants and EEG regressors encoding evidence updates at jump events (Δevidence), nor between fitted amplitude parameters (A) and any EEG regressors.
evidence: This is a negative result from correlation analysis.

claim: Participants adapted the properties of the evidence integration process to the overall statistics of the sensory environment across four different experimental conditions.
source: We found that participants' behaviour was well described by an exponentially decaying integration kernel, and that participants adapted the properties of this process to the overall statistics of the sensory environment (Ossmy et al., 2013) across four different experimental conditions.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data analysis across conditions with citation to prior work.

claim: There was substantive inter-individual variability in leaky evidence integration, with some participants rapidly discounting past evidence and others integrating over several seconds.
source: We also found that there was substantive inter-individual variability in leaky evidence integration, with some participants rapidly discounting past evidence and others integrating over several seconds.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of individual differences in integration kernels.

claim: Both sources of variability (between-condition and between-subject) were reflected by changes in centroparietal EEG responses to time-varying fluctuations in sensory evidence.
source: We then demonstrated that both sources of variability (between-condition and between-subject) were reflected by changes in centroparietal EEG responses to time-varying fluctuations in sensory evidence.
evidence: This is supported by EEG analysis showing both between-condition and between-subject effects.

claim: The P300 component has long been argued to be associated with detection of statistical surprise.
source: In particular, the well-known P300 component has long been argued to be associated with detection of statistical surprise (Donchin, 1981; Duncan-Johnson and Donchin, 1977; Mars et al., 2008; Squires et al., 1976)
evidence: This is a statement about established findings in the literature, supported by citations.

claim: The P300 has been argued to be a correlate of a continuous time-evolving decision variable that is equivalent to the CPP.
source: or, more recently, a correlate of a continuous time-evolving decision variable (Twomey et al., 2015) that is equivalent to the CPP (Kelly and O'Connell, 2013; O'Connell et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about recent theoretical interpretations in the literature, supported by citations.

claim: The centroparietal responses to |Δevidence| are consistent with a changepoint detection account of continuous decision-making.
source: Our centroparietal responses to |Δevidence| (Figure 6b) are consistent with a changepoint detection account of continuous decision-making (Booras et al., 2021), in which decision-relevant input (Figure 8) is evaluated for a change in latent state from a baseline period to a response period (Nassar et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data in relation to cited theoretical frameworks.

claim: Changepoint detection may be useful to transiently suppress neuronal activity and attend to salient incoming sensory evidence to guide choices.
source: Such changepoint detection may be useful to transiently suppress neuronal activity and attend to salient incoming sensory evidence to guide choices (Shinn et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the functional role of changepoint detection, supported by a citation.

claim: The triphasic potential is similar in timecourse and scalp topography to previous studies of evidence accumulation.
source: Alongside this, we also identify a triphasic potential that is similar in timecourse and scalp topography to previous studies of evidence accumulation (Wyart et al., 2012), sensitive to the continuous incoming sensory evidence (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings with cited prior work.

claim: The amplitude of the triphasic potential reliably predicted the time constant of leaky evidence accumulation across participants.
source: Although we did not find variation in this potential across conditions, we did find that its amplitude reliably predicted the time constant of leaky evidence accumulation across participants (Figure 9).
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral-neural correlation analysis shown in Figure 9.

claim: The pre-response central potential and centralised beta-band signals may reflect a change in decision threshold between RARE and FREQUENT conditions.
source: Relatedly, it is unclear what precise functional role of the pre-response central potential and centralised beta-band signals may play. One possibility is that they may reflect a change in decision threshold between RARE and FREQUENT conditions (Figure 7b).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the EEG findings.

claim: The authors were unable to detect any equivalent change in lateralised beta power (i.e. a signal related to the formation of a specific choice).
source: Yet we were unable to detect any equivalent change in lateralised beta power (i.e. a signal related to the formation of a specific choice Hunt et al., 2013; Kirschner et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a negative result from the analysis.

claim: One alternative possibility is that the central ERP is a readiness potential.
source: One alternative possibility is that the central ERP is a readiness potential (Schurger et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation with citation to prior work.

claim: A key advantage of continuous paradigms is that it is possible to relate time-varying properties of the continuous input to continuous output variables.
source: In addition to being more naturalistic, a key advantage of such paradigms is that it is possible to relate time-varying properties of the continuous input to continuous output variables.
evidence: This is a general statement about the advantages of continuous paradigms.

claim: Tracking paradigms have been used to dramatically reduce the length of time needed from individual participants, meaning that experiments that previously required many thousands of trials over several hours to recover psychophysical functions can now be completed in a matter of minutes.
source: This approach has been used to dramatically reduce the length of time needed from individual participants, meaning that experiments that previously required many thousands of trials over several hours to recover psychophysical functions can now be completed in a matter of minutes (Bonnen et al., 2015; Knöll et al., 2018; Straub and Rothkopf, 2021).
evidence: This is a statement about the efficiency of tracking paradigms, supported by citations.

claim: Relating continuous variations in sensory input to continuous neural signals has been shown in previous work to yield considerable improvements in signal-to-noise ratio compared to traditional trial-based event-related potentials.
source: This has been shown in previous work to yield considerable improvements in signal-to-noise ratio compared to traditional trial-based event-related potentials (Dimigen and Ehinger, 2021; Gonçalves et al., 2014; Lalor et al., 2006)
evidence: This is a statement about methodological advantages, supported by citations.

claim: The high density of events in the continuous task design (>1000 jump events in each 5 min block) limits the amount of 'dead time' present in the experimental design.
source: This efficiency is due to the high density of events in the continuous task design (>1000 jump events in each 5 min block), limiting the amount of 'dead time' present in the experimental design (Henson, 2007).
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design efficiency with citation.

claim: Inter-individual variability in integration decay time constants exceeded the between-condition variability that was observed due to experimental manipulations.
source: An intriguing finding in this work is the substantive variability in integration decay time constants across individuals. Indeed, such inter-individual variability exceeded the between-condition variability that was observed due to our experimental manipulations.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of individual differences shown in Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Different individuals might potentially achieve similar performance by ending up at very different locations in the parameter space of leak and threshold.
source: Not only does the result in Figure 4a show that behaviour should be adapted across different conditions, but it also shows that different individuals might potentially achieve similar performance by ending up at very different locations in this parameter space.
evidence: This is an inference from the computational modeling results shown in Figure 4a.

claim: During training, different participants could have optimised their parameters to maximise points gained, but in doing so ended up at different locations on the 'ridge' of parameters.
source: During training, different participants could have optimised their parameters to maximise points gained, but in doing so ended up at different locations on the 'ridge' of parameters shown in Figure 4a.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for individual differences based on modeling results.

claim: The study tested 33 participants (13 male).
source: We tested 33 participants (13 male).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the sample size.

claim: Three participants were unable to learn the continuous task and did not progress beyond training.
source: Of those, three were unable to learn the continuous task and did not progress beyond training.
evidence: This is a direct statement about participant exclusion.

claim: One participant was excluded for falling asleep during the EEG session.
source: One participant was excluded for falling asleep during the EEG session.
evidence: This is a direct statement about participant exclusion.

claim: Five participants were excluded from the analysis due to technical issues matching the continuous EEG with the stimulus stream and/or issues with EEG data quality after pre-processing.
source: Another five were excluded from the analysis due to technical issues matching the continuous EEG with the stimulus stream and/or issues with EEG data quality after pre-processing.
evidence: This is a direct statement about participant exclusion.

claim: 24 subjects were included in the analysis.
source: This means 24 subjects were included in the analysis.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the final sample size.

claim: Each subject completed six runs, except for one subject who completed only five runs.
source: Each subject completed six runs, except for one subject who completed only five runs.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data collection.

claim: For the control experiment with superimposed vertical motion, a further six participants were tested (four males).
source: For the control experiment with superimposed vertical motion (Figure 8), a further six participants were tested (four males).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the control experiment sample.

claim: All participants were aged 18–40, had normal or corrected-to-normal vision, and gave written consent prior to taking part in the study.
source: All participants were aged 18–40, had normal or corrected-to-normal vision, and gave written consent prior to taking part in the study.
evidence: This is a direct statement about participant characteristics and consent.

claim: The study was approved by the University of Oxford local ethics committee (CUREC R60298).
source: The study was approved by the University of Oxford local ethics committee (CUREC R60298).
evidence: This is a direct statement about ethical approval.

claim: Participants were faster and more accurate at detecting response periods with a higher level of average motion coherence.
source: As expected, participants were faster (F(2,46) = 29.51, p=7.45 * 10–9) and more accurate (F(2,46) = 17.6, p=0.00035) at detecting response periods with a higher level of average motion coherence (Figure 2b and c).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 2b and c.

claim: Stimulus variance during response periods impacted detection probability; response periods with a higher variance in motion coherence were less likely to be detected.
source: We found that stimulus variance during response periods did indeed impact detection probability; response periods with a higher variance in motion coherence were less likely to be detected.
evidence: This is supported by logistic mixed effects model analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The main effects of mean motion coherence, trial frequency, and trial length were left unaffected by the inclusion of the variance coregressor.
source: Crucially, however, the main effects of mean motion coherence, trial frequency, and trial length (equivalent to the effects plotted in main Figure 2b) were left unaffected by the inclusion of this coregressor.
evidence: This is supported by the logistic mixed effects model analysis.

claim: EEG data was collected at a sampling rate of 1000 Hz with Synamps amplifiers and Neuroscan data acquisition software and 61 scalp electrodes following the 10–20 layout.
source: EEG data was collected at a sampling rate of 1000 Hz with Synamps amplifiers and Neuroscan data acquisition software (Compumedics) and 61 scalp electrodes following the 10–20 layout.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the EEG acquisition methods.

claim: Bipolar electrodes were placed below and above the right eye and on the temples to measure eyeblinks as well as horizontal and vertical eye movements (HEOG and VEOG channels).
source: Additionally, bipolar electrodes were placed below and above the right eye and on the temples to measure eyeblinks as well as horizontal and vertical eye movements (HEOG and VEOG channels).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the EEG acquisition methods.

claim: A ground electrode was attached to the left elbow bone.
source: A ground electrode was attached to the left elbow bone.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the EEG acquisition methods.

claim: The EEG signal was referenced to the left mastoid but later re-referenced to the average of left and right mastoids.
source: The EEG signal was referenced to the left mastoid but later re-referenced to the average of left and right mastoids.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the EEG acquisition and preprocessing methods.

claim: Impedances of electrodes were kept below 15 kΩ.
source: Impedances of electrodes were kept below 15 kΩ.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the EEG acquisition methods.
